## 修订评估 — Reviewer 2

### 上轮 Critical 问题

**N1 (动机与范围脱节)** — **[RESOLVED]**

修改效果优异。Abstract 开篇从"training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text"改为"Recursive application of language models... produces text with progressively altered distributional properties"，紧接"restricting to base (pretrained) models to isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects"。Introduction §1 第2段明确将 base-model 定位为"deliberate design choice"并以 instruct 模型的 confounds（output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping）为依据。Conclusion 写"controlled study"。Limitations 第1段首句也改为"This is a deliberate design choice"。整篇论文的 framing 从"web curation 实用方法"转为"controlled scientific study of recursive base-model generation"，叙事一致且可信。

**N2 (方法新颖性不足)** — **[PARTIALLY RESOLVED]** ↓ 从 Critical 降为 Should-Fix

改善显著但仍有残余问题：
1. **机制假说**：Discussion 新增"Shape stationarity: mechanistic hypothesis"段，提出 softmax 架构 + sampling 超参数决定 shape、递归生成仅移动 context 进高概率区域 → location shift 而非 shape shift。这比 Round 1 的纯描述性表述有实质进步。但该假说未经正式检验（例如，通过操纵 softmax temperature 或 vocabulary size 来验证预测）。
2. **不再 overclaim**：Discussion "Comparison with detector ensembles"段明确写"We do not claim feature-engineering superiority"，Contributions 从 3 条减为 2 条。这是恰当的。
3. **Introduction 语气统一**：Introduction 第4段现在写"We hypothesize that..."而非断言，与 Discussion 的假说语气一致。
4. **残余问题**：Abstract 仍写"consistent with a location shift... that preserves its functional form"（断言性的"consistent with"而非更谨慎的"we hypothesize"），与 Introduction 的假说语气有微小不一致。但这在 convention 范围内，不升级。

---

### 上轮 Should-Fix 问题

**W1 (尺度泛化不足)** — **[STILL_OPEN]**

无新增实验。Limitations 仍写"Frontier models (70B+) remain untested"。理解资源限制下无法补做 70B 实验，但建议至少在 Discussion 中讨论一下：如果 8.2B → 0.683 的趋势外推到 70B+，方法是否还有实际意义？当前缺少对这一趋势的定量分析或定性讨论。

**W2 (Binary F1=0.723 实际效用)** — **[RESOLVED]**

新增 Discussion "Corpus-level vs. document-level utility"段，核心论点清晰："个体文档 F1=0.64 insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging"；"corpus-level estimation error scales as O(1/√n)"，类比 opinion polling。这是一个实用且有说服力的讨论，比 Round 1 有实质改善。

**残余问题**：Appendix 第22行仍写"The results are unambiguous"但紧接着报告 p=0.25——这是内在矛盾。Main text §4.4 也写"Depth-aware data curation does not improve..."作为定论式陈述。建议将"unambiguous"改为"consistent across seeds"，将 §4.4 改为"In our setting, depth-aware curation did not improve..."（过去时 + scope 限定）。

Table 1 现在包含 Binary F1 列，Caption 写"3-class results are supplementary. Binary F1 (gen-1 vs. gen-2+) is the primary metric."——presentation 问题已解决。但 §3.2 仍未解释**为什么**选择共享 seed pool 而非独立 seed pool。Method 第20-22行写"The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators. In LOGO evaluation... creating a potential train-test overlap..."，描述了问题但未给出共享设计的 rationale（是为了控制变量？还是数据约束？）。

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Recursive application of language models---where each generation step conditions on prior LLM output---produces text with progressively altered distributional properties.
We study this phenomenon under controlled conditions, restricting to base (pretrained) models to isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text by generation depth rather than a binary real-vs-synthetic label---and characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency features drift monotonically with depth while upper-tail shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution with partial shape preservation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text---estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using eight base (pretrained) models from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation; under this account, the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input content, while variance shows moderate drift.

\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Partial shape preservation: mechanistic hypothesis.}
5	Near-stationary features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain stable across generation depths ($|\rho| < 0.05$), while drifting features shift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	Entropy\_std shows moderate pooled correlation ($|\rho| = 0.200$), intermediate between the strongly drifting central-tendency features and the near-stationary upper-tail features.
7	The refined pattern is \emph{lower-tail compression with upper-tail preservation}: entropy\_min (the NLL floor) decreases with depth ($\rho = -0.406$; per-generator $|\rho|$ up to 0.51), indicating that the model's most confident predictions become progressively more confident under recursion; meanwhile entropy\_max (the NLL ceiling) is unchanged ($|\rho| = 0.050$).
8	Mechanistically, recursive generation compresses the lower tail of the NLL distribution while preserving upper-tail behavior, resulting in a net location shift with partial shape preservation.
9	The softmax and top-$p$ sampler impose an effective ceiling on per-token surprise, explaining upper-tail invariance; but conditioning on progressively more predictable context allows the model to produce increasingly confident (low-NLL) tokens, compressing the lower tail.
10	Cross-generator pooling produces minimal attenuation for entropy\_std (per-generator median $|\rho| = 0.209$, pooled $|\rho| = 0.200$), indicating consistent moderate depth sensitivity across generators.
11	This predicts that upper-tail features should remain approximately stationary until generation depth reaches the model's fixed-point distribution, a regime not yet observed in our chain lengths ($\leq$4 steps).
12	Sampling ablation is consistent with this account: depth signal is robust to moderate temperature variation (${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades substantially at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where the sampling mechanism itself becomes the dominant source of distributional shape variation, overwhelming the depth signal.
13	
14	\paragraph{Comparison with detector ensembles.}
15	On the primary binary metric (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), our 7-feature ensemble (F1\,=\,0.694) outperforms all individual detection baselines and edges out the 4-detector+surface ensemble (0.690) under 8-generator LOGO evaluation.
16	On 3-class discrimination, the multi-detector ensemble holds a slight advantage (+0.9\,pp), reflecting the additional information in combining four independent detection signals.
17	We do not claim feature-engineering superiority: the primary contributions are the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation beyond binary detection), the empirical characterization of differential depth response, and interpretability---seven summary statistics from a single lightweight reference model versus four independent detection pipelines.
18	On binary classification specifically, the 4-detector+surface ensemble achieves marginally higher pooled F1 (0.705 vs.\ 0.694), though this difference is not statistically significant (bootstrap CIs overlapping at the 95\% level).
19	That both approaches converge on near-identical binary performance suggests depth signal is accessible through multiple feature families; our approach offers a simpler, more interpretable route to the same discriminative boundary.
20	
21	\paragraph{Reference model choice.}
22	Qwen3-0.6B serves dual roles as both generator and cross-family reference model in Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}, creating a potential self-referencing bias.
23	The measured advantage is modest: Qwen3-0.6B reference achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.813 versus 0.789 for Pythia-410M (+2.4\,pp), within the range of inter-reference variation (spread 0.024; evaluated on the original 6-generator subset).
24	Qwen3-8B shows a pronounced same-family advantage under the Qwen3-0.6B reference (F1\,=\,0.757 vs.\ 0.685 with Pythia-410M), suggesting that architectural similarity between generator and reference facilitates depth signal extraction at scale.
25	All main results use Pythia-410M as the default reference to avoid this overlap; the cross-reference experiment (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) serves solely to confirm that differential depth response is reference-model-independent.
26	
27	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
28	Differential depth response strength varies substantially across prompt types.
29	Continuation chains exhibit 16.9\% depth retention loss by gen-4, while elaboration chains retain 98.6\% of samples (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
30	The 7-feature ensemble achieves within-type CV F1 of 0.781 for continuation vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration; cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal despite differing drift magnitudes.
31	Together with the paraphrastic attenuation reported below (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), these results bound depth fingerprinting's primary applicability to continuation-style generation, where distributional drift is strongest; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor as semantic-preservation constraints anchor distributional shift \cite{broken_telephone}.
32	
33	\paragraph{Corpus-level vs.\ document-level utility.}
34	The practical value of depth estimation depends on the unit of analysis.
35	At the individual document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.64 implies a 36\% misclassification rate---insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging suspect documents for human review.
36	At the corpus level, aggregate depth composition can be estimated with substantially lower error: over $n$ documents, estimation error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$---analogous to opinion polling, where individual voter prediction is unreliable but population-level estimates are actionable---making corpus-level provenance characterization reliable even with moderate per-document accuracy.
37	The 3-class design explicitly targets the most informative boundaries: human vs.\ machine (gen-0 vs.\ gen-1+) and shallow vs.\ deep recursion (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), where the distributional distinction is most actionable.
38	
39	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
40	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
41	In training-loop collapse, gradient updates on self-generated data cause progressive mode collapse---catastrophic diversity loss after 5--10 retraining generations \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
42	Our inference-chain setting involves no parameter updates; drift instead accumulates through repeated sampling from the model's high-probability regions, yielding a milder effect (hapax ratio declines ${\sim}$14\% over 4 depths).
43	Both processes share declining diversity, but they diverge in distributional shape: training collapse alters the distribution's functional form as learned parameters shift, whereas inference chains exhibit partial shape preservation---upper-tail features remain stationary because the decoding mechanism remains fixed, though variance (entropy\_std) shows moderate drift.
44	Speculatively, these trends suggest that surface features may serve as leading indicators of deeper distributional shifts, though this hypothesis requires longitudinal validation.
45	Topic drift mediates rather than confounds this process: semantic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum $R^2 = 0.082$ for entropy\_mean), and shape features are near-independent of semantic drift ($|\rho| = 0.068$).
46	
47	\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
48	Five-class depth estimation reduces macro F1 from 0.770 to 0.488 (10-fold CV, 8-generator dataset); gen-2 and gen-3 are inseparable (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.24), establishing three classes as the practical ceiling for handcrafted features (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
49	QLoRA fine-tuning raises 3-class F1 to 0.905 (+11.6\,pp over XGBoost; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.
50	
51	\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
52	Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated editing: 20\% random token replacement reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp, while LLM rephrasing drops binary F1 by 6.3\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
53	This asymmetry---surface noise is tolerable, systematic distributional manipulation is not---is consistent with depth signal residing in aggregate distributional properties rather than individual token choices.
54	
55	\paragraph{Paraphrastic chains.}
56	Initial paraphrastic experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), but removing contaminated samples aligned correlations with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
57	On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with faster convergence under semantic-preservation constraints \cite{broken_telephone}.
58	Cross-transfer is effective (para$\to$cont F1\,=\,0.770, cont$\to$para 0.743), indicating shared depth signal.
59	
60	\paragraph{Instruct tuning.}
61	Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base; Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct 0.667 vs.\ 0.816 base).
62	Length-matched controls reduce correlations to near zero (all $|\rho| < 0.02$ for Qwen3-0.6B), and binary classification is near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5), indicating that depth signal is not operationally detectable in instruct chains.
63	This justifies our restriction to base models: instruction tuning introduces distributional effects (output length regulation, format constraints) that dominate the subtler recursive drift signal, making base models the appropriate setting for isolating the generation mechanism.
64	
65	\paragraph{Negative downstream finding.}
66	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
67	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
68	The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Partial shape preservation: mechanistic hypothesis.}
Near-stationary features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain stable across generation depths ($|\rho| < 0.05$), while drifting features shift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Entropy\_std shows moderate pooled correlation ($|\rho| = 0.200$), intermediate between the strongly drifting central-tendency features and the near-stationary upper-tail features.
The refined pattern is \emph{lower-tail compression with upper-tail preservation}: entropy\_min (the NLL floor) decreases with depth ($\rho = -0.406$; per-generator $|\rho|$ up to 0.51), indicating that the model's most confident predictions become progressively more confident under recursion; meanwhile entropy\_max (the NLL ceiling) is unchanged ($|\rho| = 0.050$).
Mechanistically, recursive generation compresses the lower tail of the NLL distribution while preserving upper-tail behavior, resulting in a net location shift with partial shape preservation.
The softmax and top-$p$ sampler impose an effective ceiling on per-token surprise, explaining upper-tail invariance; but conditioning on progressively more predictable context allows the model to produce increasingly confident (low-NLL) tokens, compressing the lower tail.
Cross-generator pooling produces minimal attenuation for entropy\_std (per-generator median $|\rho| = 0.209$, pooled $|\rho| = 0.200$), indicating consistent moderate depth sensitivity across generators.
This predicts that upper-tail features should remain approximately stationary until generation depth reaches the model's fixed-point distribution, a regime not yet observed in our chain lengths ($\leq$4 steps).
Sampling ablation is consistent with this account: depth signal is robust to moderate temperature variation (${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades substantially at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where the sampling mechanism itself becomes the dominant source of distributional shape variation, overwhelming the depth signal.

\paragraph{Comparison with detector ensembles.}
On the primary binary metric (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), our 7-feature ensemble (F1\,=\,0.694) outperforms all individual detection baselines and edges out the 4-detector+surface ensemble (0.690) under 8-generator LOGO evaluation.
On 3-class discrimination, the multi-detector ensemble holds a slight advantage (+0.9\,pp), reflecting the additional information in combining four independent detection signals.
We do not claim feature-engineering superiority: the primary contributions are the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation beyond binary detection), the empirical characterization of differential depth response, and interpretability---seven summary statistics from a single lightweight reference model versus four independent detection pipelines.
On binary classification specifically, the 4-detector+surface ensemble achieves marginally higher pooled F1 (0.705 vs.\ 0.694), though this difference is not statistically significant (bootstrap CIs overlapping at the 95\% level).
That both approaches converge on near-identical binary performance suggests depth signal is accessible through multiple feature families; our approach offers a simpler, more interpretable route to the same discriminative boundary.

\paragraph{Reference model choice.}
Qwen3-0.6B serves dual roles as both generator and cross-family reference model in Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}, creating a potential self-referencing bias.
The measured advantage is modest: Qwen3-0.6B reference achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.813 versus 0.789 for Pythia-410M (+2.4\,pp), within the range of inter-reference variation (spread 0.024; evaluated on the original 6-generator subset).
Qwen3-8B shows a pronounced same-family advantage under the Qwen3-0.6B reference (F1\,=\,0.757 vs.\ 0.685 with Pythia-410M), suggesting that architectural similarity between generator and reference facilitates depth signal extraction at scale.
All main results use Pythia-410M as the default reference to avoid this overlap; the cross-reference experiment (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) serves solely to confirm that differential depth response is reference-model-independent.

\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
Differential depth response strength varies substantially across prompt types.
Continuation chains exhibit 16.9\% depth retention loss by gen-4, while elaboration chains retain 98.6\% of samples (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
The 7-feature ensemble achieves within-type CV F1 of 0.781 for continuation vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration; cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal despite differing drift magnitudes.
Together with the paraphrastic attenuation reported below (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), these results bound depth fingerprinting's primary applicability to continuation-style generation, where distributional drift is strongest; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor as semantic-preservation constraints anchor distributional shift \cite{broken_telephone}.

\paragraph{Corpus-level vs.\ document-level utility.}
The practical value of depth estimation depends on the unit of analysis.
At the individual document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.64 implies a 36\% misclassification rate---insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging suspect documents for human review.
At the corpus level, aggregate depth composition can be estimated with substantially lower error: over $n$ documents, estimation error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$---analogous to opinion polling, where individual voter prediction is unreliable but population-level estimates are actionable---making corpus-level provenance characterization reliable even with moderate per-document accuracy.
The 3-class design explicitly targets the most informative boundaries: human vs.\ machine (gen-0 vs.\ gen-1+) and shallow vs.\ deep recursion (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), where the distributional distinction is most actionable.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
In training-loop collapse, gradient updates on self-generated data cause progressive mode collapse---catastrophic diversity loss after 5--10 retraining generations \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
Our inference-chain setting involves no parameter updates; drift instead accumulates through repeated sampling from the model's high-probability regions, yielding a milder effect (hapax ratio declines ${\sim}$14\% over 4 depths).
Both processes share declining diversity, but they diverge in distributional shape: training collapse alters the distribution's functional form as learned parameters shift, whereas inference chains exhibit partial shape preservation---upper-tail features remain stationary because the decoding mechanism remains fixed, though variance (entropy\_std) shows moderate drift.
Speculatively, these trends suggest that surface features may serve as leading indicators of deeper distributional shifts, though this hypothesis requires longitudinal validation.
Topic drift mediates rather than confounds this process: semantic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum $R^2 = 0.082$ for entropy\_mean), and shape features are near-independent of semantic drift ($|\rho| = 0.068$).

\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
Five-class depth estimation reduces macro F1 from 0.770 to 0.488 (10-fold CV, 8-generator dataset); gen-2 and gen-3 are inseparable (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.24), establishing three classes as the practical ceiling for handcrafted features (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
QLoRA fine-tuning raises 3-class F1 to 0.905 (+11.6\,pp over XGBoost; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated editing: 20\% random token replacement reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp, while LLM rephrasing drops binary F1 by 6.3\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry---surface noise is tolerable, systematic distributional manipulation is not---is consistent with depth signal residing in aggregate distributional properties rather than individual token choices.

\paragraph{Paraphrastic chains.}
Initial paraphrastic experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), but removing contaminated samples aligned correlations with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with faster convergence under semantic-preservation constraints \cite{broken_telephone}.
Cross-transfer is effective (para$\to$cont F1\,=\,0.770, cont$\to$para 0.743), indicating shared depth signal.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning.}
Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base; Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct 0.667 vs.\ 0.816 base).
Length-matched controls reduce correlations to near zero (all $|\rho| < 0.02$ for Qwen3-0.6B), and binary classification is near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5), indicating that depth signal is not operationally detectable in instruct chains.
This justifies our restriction to base models: instruction tuning introduces distributional effects (output length regulation, format constraints) that dominate the subtler recursive drift signal, making base models the appropriate setting for isolating the generation mechanism.

\paragraph{Negative downstream finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive LLM generation.
In a controlled study of eight base-model generators from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency features drift monotonically while upper-tail features remain near-stationary, consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation.

These results establish depth fingerprinting as a tool for understanding recursive generation phenomena in base models.
Extending to instruction-tuned models---where depth signal degrades substantially---and frontier-scale generators (70B+) are priorities for future work.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
8	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
9	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
10	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
11	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
12	
13	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
14	\label{sec:generation}
15	
16	We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
17	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
18	
19	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
20	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
21	We use shared seeds across generators to ensure that cross-generator comparisons control for input content, isolating the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
22	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
23	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
24	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
25	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
26	The theoretical yield is $8 \times {\sim}1{,}000 \times 5 \approx 40{,}000$ texts; after removing generation failures, exact duplicates, and passages shorter than 50 tokens, 37{,}058 texts remain.
27	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
28	
29	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
30	\label{sec:features}
31	
32	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
33	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
34	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes).
35	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
36	
37	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
38	
39	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
40	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
41	Although Pythia-410M shares the GPT-NeoX architecture with two of the eight generators, cross-family reference model experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm that depth features are not reference-specific (LOGO F1 varies by only 0.024 across Pythia, OLMo, and Qwen references).
42	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:
43	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
44	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}\footnote{We use ``entropy'' as shorthand for token-level negative log-likelihood under the reference model, following convention in prior detection work. These are point-wise NLL values, not Shannon entropy of the full distribution.}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
45	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
46	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
47	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token---as generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs.
48	    Although entropy\_min shows near-zero marginal impact in leave-one-feature-out analysis ($\Delta$F1\,=\,+0.01\,pp), we retain it for completeness of the NLL summary statistics (mean, std, max, min) and because removing it does not improve performance;
49	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over $\mathcal{C}_0$), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.
50	    Sensitivity analysis confirms stable classification (F1 variation ${<}$0.3\,pp) across thresholds from the 85th to 95th percentile.
51	\end{itemize}
52	
53	\paragraph{Surface features.}
54	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
55	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
56	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
57	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
58	\end{itemize}
59	
60	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
61	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) show strong monotonic drift with generation depth ($|\rho| = 0.61$--$0.65$); entropy\_min and entropy\_std show moderate drift ($|\rho| = 0.20$--$0.41$); and upper-tail features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary ($|\rho| < 0.05$).
62	This differential behavior---consistent with recursive generation compressing the lower tail of the NLL distribution while preserving upper-tail behavior---motivates combining both feature types.
63	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.
64	
65	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
66	\label{sec:evaluation}
67	
68	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
69	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the eight generators is held out for testing and the remaining seven provide training data.
70	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
71	
72	\paragraph{Classifier.}
73	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
74	Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
75	We use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, and learning rate $0.1$ for the 7-feature ensemble.
76	Baseline detectors (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}) use the same XGBoost framework with $n\_\text{estimators}{=}100$ and $\max\_\text{depth}{=}3$ to avoid overfitting their single-feature input.
77	LOGO F1 is stable across random seeds (mean\,=\,0.762, std\,=\,0.001 over 5 seeds), confirming that results are not sensitive to classifier initialization.
78	Alternative classifiers (random forest, logistic regression) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}), confirming that discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
79	%% TODO: update ordinal method numbers from 8gen results (CORAL/Frank-Hall F1 vs 0.762 baseline)
80	We evaluated two ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall ordinal ensemble \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}); neither significantly outperforms multiclass XGBoost (3-class LOGO F1, CIs overlapping), confirming that with only three ordinal levels, ordinal structure provides minimal additional benefit.
81	
82	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
83	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.
84	We report per-class F1 scores and 95\% confidence intervals via \emph{percentile bootstrap} ($n{=}1{,}000$), resampling at the document level within each held-out fold.
85	For pairwise model comparisons (e.g., full features vs.\ ablated subsets), we use the \textbf{McNemar test} on disagreement tables.
86	For comparisons against detection baselines, we use \textbf{paired bootstrap} significance tests.
87	All reported $p$-values are two-sided.
88	We report six pairwise comparisons in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}; applying Bonferroni correction ($\alpha_{\text{adj}} = 0.05/6 = 0.0083$), all remain significant at $p < 0.001$.
89	Feature--depth correlations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) are computed on class-balanced subsamples (equal samples per depth class) to control for depth-class imbalance in the generation pipeline.
90	
91	\paragraph{Baselines.}
92	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as ordinal depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
93	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation, ensuring a controlled comparison.
94	
95	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
96	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify that depth signal is not an artifact of systematic length variation.
97	We conduct three complementary analyses: (1) Spearman correlation between text length and each feature (requiring $|\rho| < 0.15$ for non-confounded features), (2) classification with length-normalized features, and (3) comparison on length-matched subsets.
98

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrcl}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} & \textbf{Boot 95\% CI} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 & [2.335, 2.335] \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 & [2.367, 2.367] \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 & [2.387, 2.388] \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 & [2.389, 2.389] \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 & [2.681, 2.682] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds; bootstrap 95\% CI from $10{,}000$ seed-level resamples). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389). (6-generator data; fine-tuning evaluation.)}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The directional evidence is consistent: all three seeds rank the full training set above size-matched and depth-filtered alternatives, though the comparison is statistically underpowered (minimum achievable $p = 0.25$ for $n = 3$ paired comparisons).
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

A paired sign-flip test over 3 seeds yields $p = 0.25$ for size-matched vs.\ depth 0--1 ($\Delta$\,ppl\,=\,$0.020$); the test is severely underpowered (minimum achievable $p$-value with $n$\,=\,3 is $0.25$).
All three seeds show size-matched $<$ depth 0--1 (cross-seed variance $< 0.001$), providing consistent directional evidence despite insufficient statistical power.
A paired bootstrap ($10{,}000$ resamples) on the per-seed PPL differences gives a 95\% CI of $[-0.0203, -0.0193]$ for size-matched minus depth 0--1, excluding zero; the all-data vs.\ size-matched difference has CI $[-0.0326, -0.0316]$.
Cohen's $d = -34.8$ (Hedges' $g = -19.9$) reflects the near-zero cross-seed variance, not practical importance: the absolute PPL difference is 0.020 on a baseline of 2.367.

\paragraph{Statistical caveats.}
Bootstrap CIs are computed from $n$\,=\,3 seed-level aggregate perplexities; with 3 observations, bootstrap resampling produces only 10 distinct sample means, so the CIs should be interpreted as reflecting low seed-to-seed variance rather than high statistical confidence.
Document-level bootstrap (resampling over the 3{,}138 eval documents) would be more informative but requires per-sample losses that were not retained.
The extremely large $|d|$ values arise because the denominator (cross-seed standard deviation $\approx 0.0006$) is tiny; the numerator (PPL difference $\approx 0.02$) represents $<1\%$ of the baseline perplexity.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.
